comparison: Both strongly support the methodological contribution of DEMs (C29-C34). OpenEval emphasizes technical details (sample sizes, interpolation methods, smoothing kernels) while peer reviewers focus on the value as 'an important tool' for the community. Both find the approach sound and well-documented.

Perfect agreement on reproducibility analyses (C35-C41). Both evaluations find the quantitative metrics, statistical comparisons, and control analyses methodologically sound. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these findings as part of their statement that 'the methods used are solid.'

Both support ISH validation findings (C42-C44). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of qualitative and quantitative validation for V1/V2 boundaries and novel predictions. Peer reviewers find this 'convincing evidence' for relationships between gene expression maps and brain anatomy.

Complete agreement on multiscale validation (C45-C50). Both evaluations affirm the convergent evidence from cellular, histological, and neuroimaging data. OpenEval notes the APOE/AD analysis could benefit from more detail, but peer reviewers raise no concerns about these correlations.

Strong agreement on TD metric and validation (C51-C57, with peer review also covering C58-C59). Both find the statistical validation rigorous and the biological validation (recovery of classical areas, BA2/BA4 separation) compelling. Peer reviewers treat TD peaks as valid discoveries within the broader exploration of brain organization.

Both support gradient alignment findings (C58-C64) and developmental connections (C65, C138-C142). OpenEval notes C58 involves interpretation beyond direct data and appropriately flags uncertainty about directionality. Peer reviewers find the developmental evidence 'convincing' and do not challenge the authors' cautious interpretation.

Agreement on WGCNA methodology (C66-C68). OpenEval affirms quality control and reproducibility validation are sound. Peer reviewers support this as part of the broader multiscale framework, with Reviewer 3 stating 'the methods used are solid.'

Both support macroscale validation of WGCNA modules (C69-C72). OpenEval emphasizes appropriate statistical testing and specific examples. Peer reviewers recognize this as demonstrating 'the association with a large variety of maps capturing many of its microscopic and macroscopic properties.'

Agreement on microscale validation through enrichment analyses (C73-C79). OpenEval finds strong biological validation through layer and cell-type enrichments. Peer reviewers affirm this as part of the multiscale integration that constitutes a core contribution.

Both support multiscale integration demonstrated by modules (C80-C83). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of enrichment analyses spanning multiple scales. Peer reviewers recognize this as substantiating 'the genetic regulation of multi-scale aspects of the organisation of the human brain.'

Agreement on orthogonal validation methods (C84-C91). OpenEval affirms validation using meta-analytic fMRI, immunohistochemistry, and GO enrichment. Peer reviewers support this as part of the comprehensive demonstration of the framework's value.

Perfect agreement on temporal integration findings (C92-C100). Both evaluations affirm the developmental enrichment analyses using multiple independent datasets. Peer reviewers explicitly state the authors 'provide convincing evidence' for relationships 'during development.'

Complete agreement on meta-analysis integrating annotation sources (C101-C111). Both find the clustering approach appropriate and the connections to WGCNA modules validating. Peer reviewers recognize this as part of the systematic multiscale integration.

Both support disease gene enrichment findings (C112-C115). OpenEval affirms appropriate statistical testing and multiple comparison correction. Peer reviewers find 'convincing evidence' for relationships 'in the case of mental disorders,' treating this as a valid application.

Agreement on ASD gene partitioning and multiscale context (C116-C117, C122-C123, C127). OpenEval finds the recovery of known functional partitioning while adding multiscale context well-documented. Peer reviewers affirm this demonstrates how maps 'can be used to relate gene expression with... disease risk.'

Both support detailed module characterizations for ASD analysis (C118-C121, C124-C126). OpenEval finds these profiles essential to the multiscale integration. Peer reviewers recognize this as demonstrating 'the association with a large variety of maps' at multiple scales.

Agreement on ASD transcriptomic findings (C128-C129, C131). OpenEval finds statistical testing appropriate but notes C131 is interpretive. Peer reviewers affirm the ASD application as 'convincing evidence' without raising concerns about the interpretation.

Both support cortical thickness findings in ASD (C132-C135). OpenEval affirms appropriate statistical methods and quantitative significance. Peer reviewers treat this as part of the successful proof-of-principle demonstration of the framework's utility for mental disorders.

Agreement on integrated ASD interpretation (C136). OpenEval finds this synthesis well-supported by convergent evidence despite interpretive elements. Peer reviewers affirm the ASD analysis as demonstrating 'convincing evidence' for relationships in mental disorders.

Both support key methodological properties of DEMs (C137-C138). OpenEval notes these properties are demonstrated throughout the manuscript. Peer reviewers affirm the methodological contribution, with the unparcellated continuous nature being central to the 'important tool' they recognize.

Both evaluate developmental interpretation with appropriate caution (C139-C140). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to theoretical interpretation and acknowledges authors' caution about directionality. Peer reviewers find the developmental evidence 'convincing' and do not challenge the cautious framing.

Agreement on boundary detection capabilities (C143-C144). OpenEval finds strong support from V1/V2 and novel boundary validation. Peer reviewers affirm this as part of 'convincing evidence' for relationships with brain anatomy.

Both support WGCNA summary and integrative framework (C145-C146). OpenEval finds extensive enrichment analyses support the multiscale integration characterization. Peer reviewers explicitly identify this as 'the main scientific contribution' of substantiating genetic regulation of multi-scale brain organization.

Agreement on integrated ASD framework (C147-C150). OpenEval finds convergent evidence supports the synthesis despite interpretive elements. Peer reviewers affirm this integration as demonstrating the framework's ability to provide 'newly integrated multiscale understanding' of disease.

Both support the overarching multiscale framework (C147, C151). OpenEval finds this a reasonable characterization of demonstrated results. Peer reviewers explicitly recognize this as the main contribution and implicitly accept generalizability claims.

Perfect agreement on scientific context and motivation (C1-C4, C13-C17). Both evaluations find these background statements accurate and well-supported by citations. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this framing by acknowledging the scale integration challenge the work addresses.

Agreement on high-level study summary (C5-C8, with peer review covering C5). OpenEval finds these claims supported by detailed analyses throughout. Peer reviewers affirm the approach provides 'continuous maps of human brain gene expression' as an 'important tool.'

Both support summary of predictive capabilities (C6-C8). OpenEval finds these accurately characterize demonstrated findings. Peer reviewers affirm the authors 'provide convincing evidence' for these relationships across multiple domains.

Agreement on WGCNA and disease gene summary (C9-C10). OpenEval finds these accurate high-level characterizations. Peer reviewers recognize the multiscale integration as the main scientific contribution.

Both support summary of disease findings (C11-C12). OpenEval treats these as accurate summary statements. Peer reviewers affirm the framework's demonstrated utility for relating gene expression with disease risk.

Agreement on data source and output description (C18-C19). OpenEval finds these straightforward factual statements well-documented. Peer reviewers affirm 'the computation of continuous maps of gene expression for >20k genes' as 'the core methodological contribution.'

Both support validation summary (C20-C22). OpenEval finds these accurate high-level characterizations of detailed findings. Peer reviewers find the validation evidence 'convincing' for relationships with brain anatomy.

Agreement on gradient alignment summary (C23-C24). OpenEval finds this accurately characterizes detailed results. Peer reviewers affirm this as part of 'convincing evidence' for relationships with brain organization.

Both support WGCNA multiscale integration summary (C25). OpenEval finds this an accurate high-level characterization. Peer reviewers explicitly recognize this multiscale integration as the main scientific contribution.

Agreement on ASD application summary (C26). OpenEval notes some interpretive framing but finds the characterization accurate. Peer reviewers affirm the ASD analysis as a successful demonstration of the framework's utility.
Both support data sharing component (C27-C28, C152). OpenEval finds these factual statements about resources. Peer reviewers emphasize 'sharing [the maps] with the community' as a core contribution.
Agreement on resource extensibility (C153). OpenEval finds this a reasonable characterization. Peer reviewers call this 'a valuable contribution that will facilitate brain transcriptomic analyses.'

Both support forward-looking framework claims (C151, C154). OpenEval finds these reasonable characterizations of demonstrated generalizability. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these claims by recognizing the framework's broad utility.

Agreement on resource's future utility (C154). OpenEval finds this reasonable based on demonstrated results. Peer reviewers affirm this 'will facilitate brain transcriptomic analyses and the joint analyses of gene expression and structural and functional imaging.'

Both support appropriate caveats about interpretation (C141-C142). OpenEval finds these important acknowledgments of limitations demonstrating scientific rigor. Peer reviewers do not challenge this cautious framing and find the overall developmental evidence convincing.

Agreement on fetal expression validation (C65). OpenEval finds this supported by independent data despite limited scope. Peer reviewers affirm this as part of 'convincing evidence' for developmental relationships.
